newsitem.title: USA: Republican Kemp wants to heal U.S. racial divide.
newsitem.headline: Republican Kemp wants to heal U.S. racial divide.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, Political Correspondent

Republican vice presidential candidate Jack Kemp speaks with real passion about healing the racial divide that runs through America, sometimes coming close to openly contradicting his senior political partner, Bob Dole.

Kemp is engaged on what some analysts see as a hopeless task of breaking President Clinton's grip on the allegiance of black voters, more than 80 percent of whom currently support him, before the Nov. 5 presidential election.

But the former profootball quarterback and U.S. housing secretary is widely assumed to have longer-range goals, perhaps connected to his own presidential ambitions for 2000. Even if the Republican ticket headed by presidential nominee Dole loses, Kemp has already established himself as one of the frontrunners for the next election.

By visiting the black ghetto of Harlem, as he did this month, or a tough inner city Catholic school in Newark, as he did Monday, Kemp is sending a signal that he wants to remake the Republican Party as a party of compassionate, commonsense conservatism that can reach across racial barriers.

"We must set out to confront the crisis of despair in our nation's cities. We must set out to confront crime in our streets and tension between our races and ethnic groups," Kemp said Monday at Villanova University.
"You and I are called by conscience to an act of reaffirmation, of commitment and compassion -- a commitment to restore the American dream for each and every child of God."

Kemp has played the part of the loyal No. 2 on Dole's ticket -- the "blocking back" as he himself says. But even in brief speeches warming up the audience for Dole, the differences between the two can be apparent.

Addressing the root causes of crime, Kemp says too many politicians see the debate in overly simplistic terms. "The root cause of crime is not only poverty, as the Clinton administration would have us believe. Nor is it only the lack of punishment and tough laws, as some conservatives would suggest," he said.

"The root cause of crime is the wrong moral choice and the solution lies in teaching and modelling values and virtues to our children. We must combine a hope of opportunity through education, a hope of a job and a family with the certainty of punishment if we're to turn this nation around."

Contrast that with Dole's words to the same audience: "What works in combating crime is no mystery. It begins with understanding that the cause of crime can be explained with one simple word: criminals, criminals, criminals. It's time to return to what works in fighting crime -- and what works in fighting crime is fighting criminals."

Later that day, Kemp became embroiled in a long-running debate about the African proverb that became the basis of first lady Hillary Clinton's book on child rearing, "It takes a whole village to raise a child."
In his speech accepting the Republican presidential nomination in San Diego last month, Dole scoffed at the notion, saying "It doesn't take a village, it takes a family."

But when a black high school student asked Kemp for his position, the answer was different: "I personally believe that the African proverb that it takes a village has truth in it or would never have come down through the ages," he said.

"If it's good schools, if it's good neighbours, if it's a good community -- I'm convinced that if that is the definition of a village, people helping people, neighbours helping neighbours, I would accept that proverb without any problem."

Kemp originally considered running for president himself but decided against it in early 1995, saying he felt somewhat isolated in the Republican Party. He was hailed as a breath of fresh air when Dole surprisingly picked him as his running mate last month. But in many ways, Kemp remains out of step.

At Villanova, Dole unveiled a five-point anti-crime programme that called for fighting drug use, abolishing parole for violent offenders, holding juvenile criminals fully responsible for their actions, making prisoners work hard in prison and keeping guns out of the hands of criminals.
The same day, Kemp was speaking about providing jobs for felons emerging from prisons and turning inner cities into enterprise zones.

"America can do a lot better with its young people than to turn our back on what is happening in our cities, what's happening to people who no longer have jobs and do not have educational opportunity," he said. "We can do so much better in this country if we pull this nation together."
Kemp may have a tough time selling that message in 1996 but it may yet fall on fertile ground and take root for 2000.
